items.question: What did you find most valuable about visiting Chinese AI labs in person?
items.object: The value of visiting Chinese AI labs in person
items.answer: After I came back, people kept asking me, “What was your biggest takeaway from this trip?” But I think information about who is building models in AI and which teams are advancing is already relatively public. So there were not many discoveries that were like “huge scoops,” or a feeling of “I have a bold opinion.” For me, as someone who has followed these models for a long time, the more important part of the trip was meeting the people making them, understanding why they are doing this, and sensing the subtle differences. This year I have been catching up on learning about China. In the United States, many people explain Chinese teams for them, saying, “Why are they doing this?” But I wanted to hear them say for themselves, “We are here,” and “Why are we are doing these things.” That is very valuable.

items.question: Why do you think building connections between the Chinese and U.S. AI communities matters?
items.object: Connections between the Chinese and U.S. AI communities
items.answer: I will definitely continue following open-source models and trying these models. The ecosystem is very interesting right now. Many U.S. companies want to build products and services around a truly open model-intelligence stack, creating value for people across industries. Yet many of the models are built in China. These two technology communities with deep histories have historically had little overlap in how they work. Some companies also have old rules, such as Meta and Google: if you travel to China for work, your computer is basically finished. In other words, there has always been a wall in between, making it difficult for people to truly work together. But that wall is gradually being opened up now. I am very interested in that. In a sense, it is genuinely surprising that these models can be so competitive. But once you learn more about the talent and the overall ecosystem there, it also starts to make sense. A large part of why I care about AI is that I think it will bring many risks in the coming years. Especially societal risks, such as how people obtain information. Of course, it will also be an important geopolitical issue. So it is important to build bridges between people and let everyone see the real people behind these technologies, because many decisions are not made by them, even if outsiders see those decisions as highly political or extreme. Building such connections is genuinely meaningful, because this is a community moving together toward various goals, whether you call that goal AGI or something else. I am really glad to meet the people behind these technologies.

items.question: Why did your visit to China’s AI companies and research institutions leave you feeling more humble about your understanding of the country?
items.object: The limits of understanding China’s technology ecosystem through a short research visit
items.answer: As an American scientist, I do not feel qualified to offer views on China’s technology ecosystem or on China-U.S. interactions at the global level. I would say that before going, I already knew I did not understand much. After going, I felt even more strongly that there is so much more I have not seen. I only went to two Chinese cities, and it was a very intensive work trip. Much of the time, it felt as though we were being “teleported” by car from one place to another. Of course, we also had very good dinners, saw some lovely Beijing neighborhoods, and saw some old buildings. But overall, I still feel I know very little about China. If you want to form a relatively immediate, accurate intuition about a place, you need something closer to full-stack knowledge and experience. How would a person who grew up here think? What would a Chinese researcher’s instinctive reaction be? As an American, it might take me a lifetime to truly understand these things. For example, what exactly is different about the education system? When we went to Tsinghua, they also talked about an outside impression—that Chinese researchers in the past seemed less good at scientific innovation “from zero to one.” The claim itself is vague—what does zero to one mean?—but they brought it up themselves. This involves how people are trained, and how talent flows from a broader domestic network into different institutions. Hearing others talk about these things is one thing; actually seeing them on site is another. This year I read Breakneck and Apple in China, two excellent books, both about interactions between the U.S. technology ecosystem and China. But that is still only a very limited perspective. So when I left China, I felt that I had already known I did not understand much, and now I was even more certain of it. I still have a lot to learn.

items.question: Why did you find private conversations with AI researchers in China more interesting than formal company visits?
items.object: Formal company visits and private conversations with AI researchers in China
items.answer: We had hoped to talk more with researchers and establish a dialogue. At the same time, we also wanted to meet leadership as much as possible, especially leaders at startups. In practice, we mostly began by speaking with researchers, and we also met some executives. For example, people at Alibaba, or people very well known within their companies who interacted directly with founders. But in formal visits, a large part is also ceremonial: you have to show respect to the other side. That said, company leaders are usually more media-trained and sometimes say less as a result. They stick more closely to the company line, so details and nuances get flattened. So I think both situations exist. Those large companies may be more willing to let us meet senior cloud-business leaders, but they will not reveal much. There are also things I can only say were discussed privately. I do not know—maybe this is not the perfect answer, but the reality is mixed. Especially when PR and communications teams are present, most formal meeting rooms have PR colleagues in them. Some of the best conversations instead were like this: I messaged someone that I was in China, added them on WeChat, and then went out privately with a researcher for milk tea. It was not in a company conference room. Then you can directly ask, “What are you working on right now?” without that layer of— “I am sitting in the office, my manager is beside me,” and “PR is beside me” surface packaging. Those conversations are more interesting, but they were rarer on this trip.

items.question: How do you understand Chinese companies’ willingness to build their own AI models rather than use DeepSeek’s models?
items.object: Chinese companies’ pragmatic approach to building and releasing AI models
items.answer: I think I would start with a relatively easy question to answer: “Why are you releasing these models?” “Why are you building models yourselves?” “Why not just use DeepSeek’s models directly?” Many companies are very pragmatic. They say, “We need AI to serve our users, and we also want control over the entire technology stack, so we build it ourselves.” Compared with the U.S. atmosphere where “building a frontier lab is super expensive and something only a few companies can do,” Chinese companies are less intimidated about building AI models themselves. In the U.S., it may belong only to a small number of elite companies, but in China, it seems many companies will do it. That was also why we wanted to visit Meituan. We like it a lot. We did not expect that it also had its own large model, so we wanted to see what it was doing. They would say, “Yes, we need this model to support our agent products, so we built the model. We genuinely need it for product use. Whether it is open source is not the most important thing. We can also release it and get feedback along the way.” Their attitude toward “open science” is also very pragmatic.

items.question: How do you interpret Chinese AI researchers’ reluctance to elaborate on the broader social and economic effects of their work?
items.object: Chinese AI researchers’ reluctance to elaborate on AI’s broader effects
items.answer: People traveling with us would also ask broader questions, such as how AI will develop next and how it will affect the labor market and the economy. As scientists, do they feel responsible for understanding and thinking about these effects? We found that Chinese researchers were relatively less willing to elaborate extensively on their views. There are elements of corporate culture in this, but I think more importantly, their overall environment is more constrained than what is taught in schools. It is more, “I built the thing.” And China does not have as strong a podcast ecosystem as the United States, where researchers can gain recognition by increasing their visibility. Or even influence a company’s direction. The overall atmosphere is more pragmatic. When I write articles, I sometimes conflate this pragmatism with “humility.” But in fact, someone can be very humble while also simply being in an environment where they are not used to being asked certain questions.

items.question: How did you perceive Moonshot AI’s atmosphere compared with the other Chinese AI companies you visited?
items.object: The atmosphere at Moonshot AI compared with other Chinese AI companies
items.answer: I think these companies really do feel quite different when you walk into them. Kimi is an especially clear example. You get the sense that this group is very close-knit. Making something cool genuinely excites them, and so does commercializing that cool thing. Their thinking is, “We are using the models we make ourselves.” The closeness among them is something you can intuit as soon as you walk into the office. You feel that this group genuinely has strong cohesion, is very close, and is throwing itself wholeheartedly into this work together. So I would describe Kimi as the company with the “best atmosphere” among those we visited. That is, you can feel that they are quite happy and firmly following their own path. It does not feel especially corporate. When you go to Alibaba, it is obvious: this is a huge technology company, and the whole atmosphere is very corporate. Ant Group’s Bailing team has some of that feeling too, because it also belongs to a giant technology company. Among companies in between, Zhipu feels very AGI-oriented and very proud. But at least from what we encountered, it did not have the friendliness and charm of Moonshot AI. Of course, many accidental factors may be involved. After all, I only had lunch with these people for a few hours on a given day. You cannot judge a company’s long-term trajectory from that. But it is still interesting, because people express their state, and you can indeed see certain things from those states.

items.question: How do you interpret Moonshot AI having a 17-year-old high school student among the authors of its Attention Residuals paper?
items.object: Young talent at Chinese AI companies
items.answer: I think this may not be entirely unique to Moonshot AI, but rather reflect how young the talent is at these Chinese AI companies. These companies are also working to expand their presence in Western media. Many researchers are very active on X. I knew a few of them before. I get the sense that some do both product work and external communication work at their companies. For example, Crystal at Kimi and Lu at Zhipu. I met Lu. I am not sure I pronounce her name completely correctly, but she is probably only around 20 and is still in school. When she greeted me, I thought, “Wow, these people are really so young.” Another researcher we met at Xiaomi, Lai Li, seemed to be a PhD student as well as one of Xiaomi’s key researchers. Of course, the United States has people like this too—people with a lot of drive who eventually enter frontier AI labs—but in China it is so common. You keep encountering these young researchers, very young yet already deeply involved in the core work of labs. It made me feel this was somewhat of a structural phenomenon. These companies absorb young talent much faster than many other labs and are more willing to let them step forward. It is genuinely striking. I am only in my early thirties myself, and these people are really young. I usually think of myself as fairly young, but it is also cool to see that.

items.question: How do you see the differences in academic involvement in AI labs in the United States and China?
items.object: Academic involvement in AI labs in the United States and China
items.answer: One characteristic of Ai2, and perhaps one of its secrets, is that it is backed by the University of Washington. We have many PhD students participating in OLMo and other important projects. They do core work while studying. But that kind of openness is less accommodated at other labs. I know of a small number of PhD students working in labs, but in the United States they are usually the very best of the best. In China, there is much deeper intermingling with academia, especially between Tsinghua and the surrounding startups. This interaction is more intentional, and the talent overlap is greater.

items.question: Why do you think students are particularly valuable contributors to language-model research?
items.object: Students’ contributions to language-model research
items.answer: Students are young, they have drive, and they do not have much else to worry about. I am getting married this year and starting to think about family. I am 30, and there are many other things in my life to take care of. But students may think, “This is the technology I am going to work on for my whole life,” “I will keep doing it and absorb everything.” When working on language models—for example, when I work on post-training, you need to know what the pre-training team is doing, understand the multiple stages of the full training plan, and then identify and solve bottlenecks. The technical knowledge you need is actually a very large, fixed body of knowledge. If this is the most important thing in your life and you do not have many distractions, it is easier to absorb all of it. One researcher told us that new students do not have those preconceived ideas. They do not know how the old deep-learning way of doing things worked. They do not begin by thinking they need to switch to another architecture. They are more like, “I first want to know what the current state of the art is,” and “then make it better.” This is actually a simple approach that is easy to execute. Some Chinese researchers also told us, “Yes, this is what we are doing now.”

items.question: How do you see Zhipu’s position as a company compared with Kimi?
items.object: Zhipu’s corporate development compared with Kimi
items.answer: I probably did not get to know them as well as I got to know Kimi. But they are proud of their work and very successful. I think that because they went public and were suddenly put on the U.S. Entity List, they were in some sense immediately pushed into the position of a “real big company.” Kimi has not fully reached that stage. To me, the two companies are actually quite similar; they just make different model tradeoffs. If Kimi stays private while Zhipu goes public, it will be worth watching whether the cultural differences become greater as a result. Entering public markets can indeed create differences, and it usually also brings more attention.

items.question: How do you understand the demand for inexpensive open models as agents such as OpenClaw become popular?

items.question: How do you assess the strategy of large Chinese platform companies building their own AI models?

items.answer: This is indeed worth trying yourself. I think AI, because it is inherently very resource-dependent, will favor large companies more, especially those that can enter a positive flywheel. items.question: How do you understand the technology ownership mindset behind Chinese companies building their own AI models?

items.answer: I understand it as related to the super-app idea. They simply believe they can build things themselves and build them better. If it works, they keep investing, keep improving efficiency, and then tune it to their actual use cases. This resembles the path by which many Chinese domestic industries have grown into some of the world’s largest industries. If they can do something themselves, they do it themselves as much as possible rather than buying someone else’s service. That is how they can control the long-term trajectory. It is like—if I remember correctly, Wang Dan said in Breakneck that Chinese capitalism is more intense than U.S. capitalism. If you depend on someone else’s service, it is hard to truly beat them. In a highly competitive environment, you want to do everything as well as possible, and preferably do it all yourself. items.question: How do you understand Qwen’s strategy for deciding which models to release openly?
items.object: Qwen’s model release strategy
items.answer: I think Qwen earned broad recognition from the open AI community by continually releasing high-performing small models across a broad range of sizes. They were already doing this before Llama 4 came out and lost momentum. When Llama 4 was released and Meta slowed down, Qwen hit its stride. They know this too, so when we asked them, they were very focused on what developers would use. They want to keep building models that developers will use and grow on top of. But if you look at Qwen, you find that for a period it did not release its largest models. For example, Qwen Plus and Qwen Max are both closed-source. This clearly reflects Alibaba Cloud’s side. Like Google Cloud in the United States, it has enormous spending and enormous revenue. In China, Alibaba is the company most naturally suited to occupy this position. They know that too, so they will not necessarily release every model. Perhaps they will say they do not release them because nobody would use them, but I would also think, “There is a lot of money to be made here.” And there is indeed a lot of money to be made in AI. Most interestingly, many people mentioned that their focus on small models is intentional. It is not accidental. Perhaps at first it was just, “Others are doing it, so we will try it too.” But with models at 1B, 10B, and 30B scale, they have a very mature recipe. These models are very popular, and this is deliberate. Hearing them say, “Yes, this is how we do it, and we know it takes a lot of time.” So releasing models is hard and requires a great deal of work invested in the ecosystem. I think they also feel the pressure: “We can make more models, but once we release one, someone has to maintain it. We need to integrate with vLLM, integrate with all these companies, and fit into the open-source ecosystem.” The model team itself is still small and cannot outsource this work. It has to be done by the people directly involved in model development. So there is caution on both sides. On one hand, they cannot release too many models. On the other hand, they may not release the largest models because they want to monetize in the cloud.

items.question: How do you think Chinese companies will come to view spending on AI?
items.object: Chinese companies’ willingness to pay for AI
items.answer: Another question I cared about before going to China was, “Is AI spending more like SaaS software spending, or more like cloud spending?” There is a view in the United States, whether stereotype or reality, that Chinese companies are less willing to pay for this kind of software service. For example, equivalents to Slack are much smaller. Many companies may rebuild a minimum viable piece of software themselves, or download open-source tools, rather than pay monthly per person or per seat for software. But these companies all use cloud services. Alibaba Cloud itself is a large business, and much modern software must run through the cloud. I think China will gradually view AI spending as cloud spending. It may not be as extreme as in the United States, but it will be seen as an investment necessary to make the technology they want. Therefore, these cloud providers will exist. This is interesting because when you arrive at Shanghai airport or take the high-speed rail to Hangzhou, you see Alibaba Cloud billboards everywhere.

items.question: How do you understand the differences between the U.S. and Chinese markets for AI cloud services?
items.object: U.S. and Chinese AI cloud-services markets
items.answer: I think one difference between Alibaba Cloud and Amazon Web Services is that AWS Bedrock hosts nearly all large models, including its own models and smaller models, whereas Chinese cloud providers usually host only their own models. This is a major difference. And I think the United States has a new cloud-services market, with many companies reselling other people’s models by token or reselling compute. This is a large part of the U.S. market. You can name many companies. CoreWeave, Nebius, Together, Fireworks, Lambda, and so on. This layer is much more open. We also discussed OpenRouter. I do not know whether China has a true equivalent. I do not think it does. These U.S. companies are in many ways seen as backed by NVIDIA. NVIDIA wants the ecosystem to be more diverse, because if most of its revenue comes only from a small number of companies such as OpenAI, that is not good for it. China does not seem to have exactly the same dynamic.

items.question: How do you assess the prospects for B2B AI partnerships in China?
items.object: The prospects for B2B AI partnerships in China
items.answer: This returns to whether these partnerships can form. I think many companies are considering whether they can enter the global B2B enterprise-software market. Of course, you can bring AI expertise into another company, and that would be valuable for companies with weaker AI capabilities. But the question is: are people willing to do that? items.question: How do you view the decision by companies like 01.AI and Databricks to stop developing their own AI models?
items.object: 01.AI and Databricks stopping model development
items.answer: I think there are many opportunities in AI, but building models is a completely different culture. Building models is like continuously turning a machine and constantly adding resources. I do not think 01.AI is simply a case of “it made a model and then stopped.” There are similar situations in the United States. For example, Databricks made models, and later it may have thought, “We do not need to keep doing this; others have already made it work.” Although I am not sure whether that is a public statement, I imagine many people in Databricks management think, “We are happy not to spend money training models ourselves. We will focus on our core business.” That is also why I am surprised that so many companies are still continuing to increase their investment, thinking about building trillion-parameter-scale MoE models. That is much more expensive. 01.AI and Databricks exited at the stage of smaller mixture-of-experts models or smaller dense models, where the investment was much lower. From one perspective, if you judge that you will not be competitive, stopping early may actually be wise.

items.question: How do you assess the performance gap between leading U.S. and Chinese AI models?
items.object: The performance gap between leading U.S. and Chinese AI models
items.answer: On traditional benchmarks, the gap has been roughly six to nine months for some time. But in real use, especially in the early days of reasoning models, the gap was very close, because that was a new paradigm. In a new paradigm, the gains from improvement are very steep. Both U.S. and Chinese labs are climbing quickly, and Chinese labs release faster. When you talk to people at Chinese labs, they say—our model is still undergoing reinforcement learning; the final round of reinforcement learning will run for about a week, and then it will be released within a day after completion. U.S. labs usually have a process where it takes weeks before a model can be released. So this is rapid growth, with two different curves. If China is behind, it is not in a phase of zero progress. The flat phase is the waiting period before release. So China releases faster, which narrows the performance gap that users get. Ultimately, the performance gap is the gap between models that people can use. We also discussed the knowledge-work domain. This mainly involves U.S. workers. I think U.S. frontier models are more robust in their raw usefulness in these real-world settings, but that is hard to measure. So on popular benchmarks, the six-to-nine-month gap may remain relatively stable, but on some intangible, hard-to-measure dimensions of use, U.S. models may pull ahead. The best example is the programming revolution involving Claude Code and Codex—starting in December and January. If an open-weight model could support the same behavior, the entire world would talk about it. I would pay one dollar per month rather than $200 to OpenAI, and many people would switch. Right now I would say five or six months. I do not expect a very clear watershed moment this year that will make us rethink the gap. The way we currently look at the gap may be too narrow for the scenarios in which AI is now widely used.

items.question: How do you understand the gap between Chinese AI coding models and U.S. coding assistants such as Claude Code and Codex?
items.object: Chinese AI coding models and U.S. coding assistants
items.answer: A major reason Claude Code and Codex are popular is that they are very easy to use. I think Chinese teams will continue solving coding ability. The models’ actual code quality will be very high, because this can be based on public data, GitHub, and so on. Models can learn to solve problems through tasks. But on “ease of use,” U.S. labs have a large lead, and their operating models are different. U.S. labs can obtain consumer data. For example, Cursor can train models on data from users using Cursor. This is also a huge advantage of closed labs.

items.question: How do you understand Chinese AI labs’ strategy of releasing powerful open-source models?
items.object: Chinese AI labs’ strategy of releasing powerful open-source models
items.answer: This is their path to relevance. I think they know they are behind, and they know they want to enter the conversation. items.question: Why do you see NVIDIA as the best hope for the United States to regain leadership in open AI models?
items.object: NVIDIA’s role in restoring US open-model leadership
items.answer: Because the United States has NVIDIA, and NVIDIA’s financial interest is not in having AI owned by any single company. The best way to achieve that is to release open models for the world. So the only hope is NVIDIA. Realistically, perhaps. With open models, companies such as Meta and Microsoft have products, whether consumer-facing or enterprise-facing, that are supported by AI. So they can release open-weight models without truly affecting their businesses. But in recent years they have chosen not to do so. Perhaps it would distract attention; perhaps there are marketing or safety risks. As long as this remains the case, I think NVIDIA is the party best positioned to change the situation.

items.question: How do you assess NVIDIA’s progress in open models following the Nemotron 3 Ultra release?
items.object: NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 series and its prospects for sustained progress
items.answer: While we were recording this episode—just a few days ago, I think—Jensen Huang released their Nemotron 3 Ultra model. I think this means NVIDIA has completed the first phase of trying open models again. They released the Nemotron 3 Nano, Super, and Ultra series, using mixture-of-experts models. Ultra is the largest one. Next, they will use it to generate synthetic data, build various smaller models internally, and distill. Now that they have their first large model, they have more flexibility to build other sizes and keep improving. So NVIDIA’s next moves in open models will be worth following more closely. The question is, once someone has built this big mixture-of-experts model, can they continue scaling it up from there? NVIDIA has also had many models in the past that were good quality but quickly fell out of the usage and discussion cycle.

items.question: What strategy do you think organizations such as Reflection AI and Ai2 should pursue in open models?
items.object: Model-building strategies for Reflection AI and Ai2
items.answer: Reflection AI wants to make large models, but it has to compete with Qwen, and Qwen has already earned recognition. Its models are not huge, but researchers around the world use them as a foundation. How much AI research now uses Qwen as a base is unbelievable. For a long time it was Llama, but now everyone—every researcher—understands how Qwen works and is used to using it. That is an extraordinary achievement for Qwen. I think it is not discussed enough. Over time, there will be more layered interest across the distribution of models from small to large. For Reflection AI, it may be better to choose an underserved niche. Ai2’s small OLMo models are very helpful for research. I do not think Ai2 should chase the frontier and build trillion-parameter models. That is not feasible from a philanthropic-funding perspective either. But it is also good to do things that are strategically different. Before everyone realizes they can no longer financially keep up with the frontier, there is time to fill different niches.

items.question: Which Chinese open-source models do you currently regard as the strongest?

items.answer: The ranking goes back and forth. I myself want to spend more time trying different models. items.question: What differences stand out to you between Chinese and U.S. AI research labs?
items.object: Chinese and U.S. AI research labs
items.answer: I think China has a great deal of talent. When you enter a lab, you find that most people are researchers who grew up in China, and they are often younger. We went to many places near Tsinghua. Of course, China has other excellent universities too. So when you enter Chinese labs, the makeup of personnel is more homogeneous. By comparison, at Ai2 and other U.S. labs, as an American who is not an immigrant and whose parents are not immigrants, I sometimes feel a little unusual myself. I work with people from all over the world—Europe, the Middle East, China, and other parts of Asia. U.S. labs are like this too; they have many Chinese researchers. But in terms of the overall demographic makeup, the feeling on site is very different. Another difference is one we mentioned earlier: when many top U.S. researchers discuss questions like “where AI is going,” they focus more on the philosophy behind models or artistic design ideas. An example was raised by Caithrin Rintoul, the organizer of this trip. She pointed out that discussions such as Amanda Askell talking about a model’s temperament and carefully shaping its tone do not really appear in China. There are some local discussions in China, but what topics they are willing to discuss, and how far they are willing to project AI’s future, are very different from the United States. Beyond that, they are actually very similar.

items.question: How do you compare the intellectual outlook of young Chinese AI researchers with the outlook you encounter in Silicon Valley?
items.object: Chinese researchers’ intellectual outlook compared with Silicon Valley’s AI culture
items.answer: A more interesting and distinctly Chinese point is that the newest generation of Chinese researchers seems to have better English. Many very young people have excellent English and closely follow the Western AI ecosystem. They are on Twitter and blogs, and they write papers. But the reverse is not true. In the U.S. ecosystem, many people do not care about what is happening in China and do not really understand how China’s technology ecosystem operates. Even for someone like me who is very interested and wants to know how these companies operate, it is difficult to obtain reliable information. So information flows are very asymmetric in the two directions. That affects how people think. There is also a very typical American character here: being extremely proud of what is happening around oneself, even somewhat self-intoxicated. Silicon Valley especially rewards this kind of expression. Silicon Valley is developing a kind of “tunnel vision.” It is developing its own increasingly narrow culture and discussion around AI. For example, strange arguments about a “permanent underclass,” and current talk about recursive self-improvement in the technological singularity. You occasionally hear a little similar discussion in Chinese labs, but much less. They may receive some of it from the United States and think it is a bit strange, though also interesting enough to listen to. But when you go to San Francisco, people there really are talking about these things. You see PhD students saying, “I need to make money quickly now. I need to get into a lab.” There is a very strong culture and anxiety around AI timelines and career changes. China feels different. They are more like, “We are going to build this thing.” In some sense, they are more grounded and less anxious.

items.question: Why do you see building language models as an organizational-design problem?
items.object: Organizational design in language-model development
items.answer: I think the vision itself is difficult. One frequently underestimated part of making language models is that it is, to a large extent, an organizational-design problem. You have a lot of talent and want to make the model better. The real difficulty is how to organize those people, how to break a big problem into many smaller ones, and how to have large amounts of talent contribute toward improving the same model. I am still not sure whether I want to state this judgment too absolutely, but one possibility is that Chinese engineers’ training may indeed be more suited to this organizational model: each person repeatedly refines their small piece and accepts that it ultimately contributes one part to the larger model. Of course, there is still much uncertainty here. Because how frontier labs really operate internally has not been well documented. Maybe the reality is messier: a group of people running around trying to find ways to make the model better. This analogy may not be perfect, but it is certain that the work is heavily constrained by organizational capacity. You have to organize so many people effectively around the same goal.

items.question: Why do you think China’s education system may make it harder to cultivate truly visionary researchers?

items.question: How do you assess the possibility that Chinese AI labs will surpass U.S. AI labs?
items.object: Chinese AI labs’ prospects of surpassing U.S. AI labs
items.answer: What people are debating now is whether their repeated refinement of these fundamental things is enough to allow them to—everyone is guessing, “Will China surpass U.S. AI labs?” I think if resources were completely equal, they might be able to. Or perhaps they simply have more talent willing to invest more time over five to ten years. But I think talent is only one part of the resources needed to make models. items.question: How do you view Chinese AI researchers developing public influence outside their companies?
items.object: Chinese AI researchers developing public influence outside their companies
items.answer: After entering the Western ecosystem, I think some Chinese researchers will find that they are actually well suited to this environment. items.question: How do you assess Chinese AI labs’ approach to alignment and safety?
items.object: Chinese AI labs’ approach to alignment and safety
items.answer: The term they use more often is security. Companies certainly care about these things, but it is not their highest priority. Their thinking is more like: if we release model weights, we need to make sure they do not create some huge new risk. We also press them with questions such as, what about multimodal models? They acknowledge that some things may become risks more quickly, but they do not have that kind of strong narrative—namely, that the LLM agents we are about to release are a major risk and therefore must be banned from release. Their answers to these questions are reasonable, but unlike in the United States, where this discussion can sometimes be almost ideological, with a deep concern that the next generation of AI may be the thing that truly warrants the highest vigilance. So I think Chinese labs have a measured attitude, but this issue is not put front and center. Chinese companies may be more pragmatic. items.question: How do you think powerful AI models should be released to the public?

items.answer: I support open models, but I am not an absolutist. I do not think every model necessarily should be open. For example, Claude Mythos—of course, in some ways there is a marketing component to it—but it really is also a very major breakthrough. If it were uploaded to Hugging Face on the first day it was made, that might not be a good thing. Technology diffusion inherently needs time, especially for technology that could have such an enormous impact. Gradual diffusion over time is reasonable. With closed models currently leading and open-source models following behind, I think that is actually a fairly good way to let the technology gradually enter the real world. items.question: How do you understand the way compute constraints shape Chinese AI labs’ model design decisions?
items.object: Model design under compute constraints at Chinese AI labs
items.answer: I think most importantly, every model is basically designed around the downstream use you expect and the shape of your training cluster. The training cluster determines the efficiency of training models at different scales, and you also know that you need to serve the model afterward. Because they may have smaller training clusters, that changes many decisions. It may also make them less likely to change the base model architecture, because pretraining runs will take longer. This is more pronounced for smaller labs. Alibaba and ByteDance are somewhat special because of the scale of their resources, but labs like MiniMax and Moonshot AI... People generally believe that Claude- and GPT-level models are roughly in the range of 3 to 6 trillion parameters. If they cannot get resources such as the latest NVL72 racks and Blackwell chips, it will be harder for them to keep scaling up, so they will have a ceiling. But this is also a multi-objective optimization problem. What is your training cluster? What is your inference stack? Do you want it to run on Huawei inference chips now? Who are your users? All of these affect the design. What we ultimately see is just a 600-billion- to 1-trillion-parameter model on Hugging Face. The mapping behind it is very complicated, but I think this is one of a lab's most interesting decisions, and most people will not tell you the details.

items.question: How do you think compute scarcity shapes the way AI labs pursue efficiency?
items.object: Compute scarcity and AI labs’ pursuit of efficiency
items.answer: I would say it changes how you work. Everyone wants compute efficiency, because if your research efficiency is higher and you cut the cost of an experiment in half, you can run twice as many experiments. This is very basic math that every AI researcher wants. It is hard to say Chinese labs are necessarily better at efficiency. Perhaps because they have less inference compute, they will train models that are more inference-efficient, but that is another trade-off. DeepSeek is known for some innovations that save memory, some of which are now widely adopted. But from the perspective of American labs, that kind of optimization can sometimes also look like overkill. It can bring a small gain, but may not be worth investing so much effort in.

items.question: How do you assess the practical usefulness of Huawei chips for language-model inference and training?
items.object: Huawei chips for language-model inference and training
items.answer: The view that inference is basically usable but training is not yet viable is basically the consensus. We went to some less central companies—not core LLM companies—and they would say, “Yes, we need Huawei chips, but we have not used them much yet.” But most language-model companies we spoke with are already mature enough: they have services, and people are signing up to use them. For example, Zhipu's API processes trillions of tokens every day. So these companies all say, “If you can give me Huawei chips, maybe we can get more customers.” They are figuring out how to use Huawei chips for inference, but for training, currently only very small models may be trained on Huawei chips. Personally, I expect this situation to continue for a while.

items.question: How do you assess Huawei’s prospects for catching up with NVIDIA in chips for AI training?
items.object: Huawei’s progress toward competing with NVIDIA in AI training chips

items.question: Where do you stand in the debate between Jensen Huang and Dwarkesh over restricting NVIDIA GPU sales to China?
items.object: The Jensen Huang–Dwarkesh debate over restricting NVIDIA GPU sales to China
items.answer: Realistically, I am in the middle, but lean more toward Dwarkesh. Ultimately this becomes a geopolitical discussion: do you believe AI will be used in competition for national power? As an American, I would prefer traditional American values, such as freedom of expression, to spread more throughout the world. I also think providing AI chips to China does create some risks to the balance of power. So, as an American, that is roughly where I would stand. But the question of degree is hard to judge. When you listen to people inside NVIDIA, they basically say the United States no longer has more electricity to build data centers, so there is nobody in the United States who can buy these chips. They want to sell them to China. But at the same time, American companies are asking for more allocation. U.S. policymakers also hear American companies saying they would buy more. So I have spoken to both sides. American labs say, “I want more chips to grow my company.” NVIDIA policy researchers say, “The United States cannot accommodate more volume.” It is hard to get the real data. How many chips would the United States actually buy, and how many chips have been diverted to the Chinese market? That is also why I have so much uncertainty about this issue. I do not know where the ultimate balance point lies. So perhaps there really are some chips that NVIDIA simply cannot sell in the United States, and maybe we should allow them to sell those to China to support NVIDIA in maintaining AI leadership. But I cannot say for sure.

items.question: Do you think restrictions on China's access to NVIDIA GPUs will spur China to develop better domestic AI chips?
items.object: The effect of GPU export restrictions on China's domestic AI chips and infrastructure
items.answer: That will definitely happen. I think AI will be more like cloud spending. This will support all kinds of new companies in China, because they need cloud resources to build viable products, and it will also bring growing inference demand. OpenClaw and Claude Code both show that inference demand already exists. Adoption in China is still earlier-stage. When you talk to Chinese developers, they say, “I use Claude,” which means that demand is currently being routed to Western compute. As China unlocks more domestic AI inference capacity, the demand from these use cases will converge on one question: how many chips can Huawei make? So this is not something that will happen years from now; it will happen within months. China will have new applications, like Claude Code, that enormously empower developers. People will have very strong demand for them. So I really do see this happening. From that perspective, Jensen Huang is partly right. It will drive the development of the domestic AI stack. Domestic labs already have Huawei chips and are designing inference solutions for them. In a sense, it is already happening. The remaining questions are how large the scale will be, and how much people consider acceptable.

items.question: Why do you see China's underdeveloped AI training-data industry as such an important difference from the United States?
items.object: The gap between China's and America's AI training-data industries
items.answer: One of the things that surprised me most is that China's data industry is far less developed than America's. In the current American environment, companies like Anthropic and OpenAI say they have data budgets in the billions of dollars to buy training environments from external vendors. We asked Chinese companies, and they said, “No, we basically do not have that.” Some do it internally. People mention companies such as ByteDance and Alibaba, which are larger and can build internal data teams. But almost nobody says, “We go to an external supplier and buy some data,” whereas this is very common in the United States. It is almost the standard playbook for frontier labs. To put it realistically, training a model sometimes means identifying what the model is bad at, buying data for that area, and seeing whether you can improve performance. Of course they also do more exciting research, but this boring data engineering is very important. And this dynamic seems not to exist in China. This is the biggest difference I have seen. OpenAI researchers of course have more compute than Chinese researchers, so Chinese startups may work on different problems and appear more efficient. But data is not inherently something that has to be different, yet it really is very different.

items.question: How do you understand the role of domestic demand in building the specialized training-data industry that Chinese AI agents need?
items.object: The relationship between domestic AI-agent demand and a specialized training-data market
items.answer: The current understanding of American frontier models is that they will enter knowledge-work tools. As a typical knowledge worker myself, I now use Claude Code and Codex for most of my work. People will see them enter fields such as medicine, law, consulting, and finance. Much of the training data for these models in those fields is obtained through a network of data companies. They pay professionals to create training data. The United States has a complete market: Scale AI, Mercor, Surge, Turing, and many other companies. The market is driving them to shift from offshore preference data for reinforcement learning from human feedback toward an industry of highly skilled labor. It is enormous. The various model labs pay billions of dollars for this. They do it because it genuinely has value: it makes models stronger on these agentic tasks. So the question is whether Chinese labs can open up the domestic market for their agents. If people really use their models to do these things, demand will give them the ability to buy this expensive data. Conversely, if Chinese AI researchers and knowledge workers all say, “I use Claude,” then Claude has even more reason to keep doing these things in the United States, and the data industry will continue to remain in the United States. I talk to friends doing post-training in labs, and they say that the incremental performance gains obtained by these data companies in every domain are really important. If China does not have such an industry, it has to be very creative. You might have AI researchers construct a financial-task environment themselves, for example, making Excel spreadsheets. But that is not a task AI researchers are naturally good at. That is another world.

items.question: How do you compare the U.S. and Chinese software ecosystems as environments for developing new AI applications?
items.object: U.S. and Chinese ecosystems for new AI applications
items.answer: I think both the United States and China will be especially active at the application layer. Some might even say American consumers are more accustomed to downloading new apps, using them, and paying for them, while China has these super-apps. The question is, “Can super-apps support an equally diverse range of new application scenarios?” In the United States, you see a product like Sora suddenly become number one, with millions of people trying it, and then perhaps fall from its pedestal again. It has its own sandbox and can offer a more defined experience. So I think at the software layer, the U.S. ecosystem is better suited to rapid experimentation and rapid iteration for new applications.

items.question: Why do you expect American startups building on open-source AI models to visit Chinese labs and develop closer relationships with them?
items.object: Cross-border collaboration between American open-source AI startups and Chinese labs
items.answer: I think some American companies—especially small and medium-sized players creating economic value around open-source models, whether they make fine-tuning APIs or specialized deployment services, and so on—will want to build relationships with Chinese labs, because Chinese labs are very willing to share technology and experience. After I went to China, many companies came to ask me, for example, “How did you get in touch with those labs? We want to go too.” If you look at American companies doing infrastructure or model training, they are building on open-source models. If this trend continues, we will enter a new era in which these new companies begin to learn cross-border collaboration. I expect more American companies will go to China, because visas are much easier now. I used transit visa-free entry, where you enter and leave via different countries. It was very simple; basically, you just arrive. By contrast, Chinese researchers or engineers going to the United States have to wait through the visa process. So I expect more mid-sized American startups interested in open-source models to go to China. This should happen in the next few weeks to months. Things like this move quickly. Summer 2026.

items.question: How do you expect AI technology to develop over the next twelve months?
items.object: AI products and technical progress over the next twelve months

items.question: How do you assess AI labs’ business prospects over different time horizons?
items.object: AI labs’ business prospects over short and long time horizons
items.answer: I lean toward thinking that we will see revenues continue growing for AI labs large and small. OpenAI and Anthropic may go public, and that will be fine. But the more interesting ones are mid-sized companies... such as Together, Fireworks, Baseten, and some Chinese labs such as Kimi, Zhipu, and MiniMax. They are not as gigantic, but they will sell tokens, models, and all kinds of intelligent services. They will also perform well at “selling intelligence,” because demand is so large. Twelve months is still a very short period. We are still seeing demand rise rapidly. The market will probably still be very crazy, or perhaps we have not yet reacted—we have not fully absorbed this demand cycle. So it may still look like a continuation of the current trend. items.question: How do you view the global AI race after your trip to China?
items.object: The global AI race after Nathan Lambert’s trip to China
items.answer: I am probably fairly neutral. My main concern about AI is that U.S. public opinion may become more negative toward AI, and that could harm progress. items.question: How do you understand Ai2's research culture?
items.object: Ai2's research culture
items.answer: At Ai2, we do all kinds of open AI research and development. It used to be academically oriented, and over time it has increasingly shifted toward this kind of “artifact-centered” development: you produce models, code repositories, and datasets so the entire community can keep building on top of them. OLMo and these open language models are among the most popular ones... But there are also the Molmo multimodal model, OlmoEarth, and so on. In addition, Ai2 has long been widely known for its “integration with the academic literature.” The application in this area is Semantic Scholar, which is in some ways viewed as an alternative to Google Scholar for searching academic literature. items.question: How do you see research freedom at Ai2 compared with academia and closed AI labs?
items.object: Research freedom at Ai2 compared with academia and closed AI labs
items.answer: On the spectrum from closed labs to academia, in terms of resources we are in the middle. In terms of freedom, we have more resources, but there is also pressure: we have to make models that are genuinely useful. So that does somewhat suppress freedom, but nowhere near as much as at a frontier lab racing toward AGI. Still, if you walk into a real academic institution, you see a diversity and spark of ideas that you do not get in companies. Companies cannot avoid having to make money to pay the bills.

items.question: How do you find Seattle’s atmosphere compared with Silicon Valley’s?
items.object: Seattle’s atmosphere compared with Silicon Valley’s
items.answer: It is much calmer here. There are not many social events. I actually wish Seattle had more people gathering. There are several important concentrations of tech talent here, such as Amazon and Microsoft; the major tech companies should get together more. But that is just the reality—there is nothing to be done. In some ways... I think it is better suited to settling down and starting a family, because there is more space and life is not as tense. The overall atmosphere is quite nice. Here, you do not talk about AI everywhere you go, while in the Bay Area, AI now feels like the only topic. I understand why. I believe in this stuff myself, too.
